job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Issues in S. 2817 (as amended Oct. 6, 2026)

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A): per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton limit applies "by a single vessel." An operator could stay under the cap on each of several vessels and recover any total amount without violating the Act.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "per year" undefined.** The text doesn't say whether this means a calendar year, a fiscal year, or any rolling 12-month period. It also doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry, a difference that is large for water-saturated nodules. Each choice moves the threshold and gives defendants room to argue.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "recovery" undefined.** It's unclear whether recovery means collecting material on the seafloor, lifting it to the surface, or landing it in port. Material collected but left on the seabed, or transferred at sea, may fall outside the definition.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "other mineral resources" and "seabed" are open-ended.** Read literally, this could cover offshore sand and gravel or even oil and gas in deep water, which invites overbreadth challenges. The 200-meter depth also has no stated reference point, such as mean sea level or a tidal datum.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B): "the Secretary" is never defined.** The Act doesn't say whether this means Commerce, Interior, or another department, so no agency clearly holds the power. That gap invites challenges to any determination made under it.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B): open-ended delegation with criminal consequences.** The Secretary can make "any activity" a crime under Sec. 5(b) with no rulemaking procedure, notice, or standard beyond "comparable" risk. This is exposed to vagueness and fair-notice challenges, and to delegation-based challenges.

7. **Sec. 2(2): narrow "U.S. person" definition.** It covers citizens and corporations "organized under the laws of a State." That arguably leaves out LLCs and partnerships, entities organized in DC or the territories, and lawful permanent residents. It also has no ownership-or-control test, so a U.S. company can operate through a foreign subsidiary, including one sponsored by a foreign state.

8. **Sec. 2(3): covered-vessel threshold doesn't match the prohibition.** Registration applies only to vessels over 5,000 gross tons, while the mining definition uses a tonnage cap on recovered material. Smaller vessels can mine without registering. "Equipped for" recovery is also undefined: does it mean permanently fitted, or carrying removable gear?

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

9. **Sec. 3(a): "person" and "in the United States" undefined.** The text doesn't say whether "in the United States" includes the territorial sea, the EEZ, or the continental shelf, which is central to where seabed mining would actually happen.

10. **Sec. 3(a): only direct mining is covered.** "Engage in" doesn't clearly reach financing, chartering, contracting, processing, or buying minerals mined by others. There is no import ban, so U.S. firms could buy or process nodules recovered by foreign operators.

11. **Sec. 3(a): possible overreach to individual crew.** "Any U.S. person anywhere" could expose individual American employees on foreign-flagged vessels to criminal liability. Critics could cite this as overbroad, and the government may be reluctant to enforce it.

12. **Sec. 3(b): grandfather clause may swallow the rule.** It exempts "mining conducted under an exploration license," but exploration licenses don't authorize commercial recovery. The clause could therefore be read to turn exploration rights into commercial-mining rights. The text also doesn't say which license regime counts: Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA) licenses, International Seabed Authority (ISA) contracts, or foreign-state licenses.

13. **Sec. 3(b): no limits on grandfathered operations.** There is no expiration date, no cap on scope or tonnage, and no rule on renewals, extensions, modifications, or transfers. Grandfathered status could be sold or expanded indefinitely.

14. **Sec. 3(c): environmental-assessment exemption has no limits.** "Activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment" is undefined, self-declared, and uncapped, with no permit, oversight, or reporting requirement. A commercial operation could be labeled a "pilot" or "assessment" program.

## Sec. 4: Registry

15. **Sec. 4: no penalty for failing to register or report.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so the registration and reporting duties can't be enforced under the Act itself. A false certification might still be prosecuted under the general federal false-statements law, 18 U.S.C. § 1001.

16. **Sec. 4(a): no deadline, scope, or definition of "operator."** The Act doesn't say when registration is due or whether it applies to foreign-flagged vessels operating near U.S. waters. "Operator" (owner, charterer, or master?) is undefined.

17. **Sec. 4(b): reports lack required content and verification.** The reports need not include tonnage, location, depth, or dates. They are self-certified with no audit, inspection, or vessel-tracking requirement. Without tonnage data, the per-vessel cap in Sec. 2(1)(A) can't be monitored.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

18. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8: conflicting start dates.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days after enactment. Defendants can argue the two provisions conflict and nothing is unlawful until the effective date. At minimum, the conflict creates confusion.

19. **Sec. 5(a): per-day penalty doesn't fit an annual threshold.** A violation exists only once more than 10,000 tons are recovered in a year. It's unclear which "days" count as violations: only days after the threshold is crossed, or the whole year in hindsight.

20. **Sec. 5: no enforcement machinery.** No agency is designated to enforce. There is no administrative penalty process, investigative or boarding authority, forfeiture of vessels or recovered minerals, injunctive relief, or citizen-suit provision.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

21. **Sec. 6: hortatory and ambiguous deadline.** "Seek to negotiate" creates no enforceable obligation. "Not later than 18 months" could mean start or finish negotiations. There is no reporting requirement to Congress, and no mention of the ISA or of the fact that the U.S. isn't a party to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.

## Sec. 7: Duration

22. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b): which governs?** Subsection (a) says the ban lasts until Congress acts, while (b) ends the whole Act after 10 years regardless. The two give contradictory accounts of the ban's duration.

23. **Sec. 7(a): largely illusory mechanism.** A joint resolution is itself a law needing presidential signature, which Congress could pass at any time anyway. The Act also never directs the National Academies (NASEM) to produce the report, and "serious harm" is undefined.

24. **Sec. 7(b): no savings clause.** When the Act "cease[s] to have effect," pending enforcement actions for past violations may abate. The 10 years also run from enactment, not the effective date, so the ban operates for about 9.5 years.

## Sec. 8 and Structural Issues

25. **Sec. 8: 180-day ramp-up window.** Operators can mine, stockpile, or reposition assets offshore and into foreign structures before the ban bites, subject to the conflict noted in item 18.

26. **No relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend, repeal, or override DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.), under which NOAA can issue commercial recovery permits. A permit holder could argue that existing federal authorization conflicts with or limits the ban.

27. **No rulemaking authority, severability clause, or judicial-review provision.** Without severability, a successful challenge to a vulnerable provision like Sec. 2(1)(B) could put the whole Act at risk. Without rulemaking authority, the agency can't fill the many definitional gaps above.

---

**Notes for coverage:**
- This is a textual analysis, not a legal opinion. Please check it against the official manager's amendment text before publishing.
- Many of these points cut both ways. Some make the ban weaker (items 1, 7, 12, 14), while others make it broader or more legally vulnerable (items 4, 6, 11).
- For our nonpartisan framing, it may help to present these as "questions the committee may face" and seek comment from the sponsor's office and from industry and environmental stakeholders.
